knowledge_point.title: Calculating a Definite Integral of a Rational Function Using Substitution

question.:question/worked-solution:
We start by changing the variable:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =2 x + 9 \\ \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =2 \\ \text{d}u & =2\,\text{d}x \\ 1\,\text{d}u & =2\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=2 x + 9.$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & -1 & 0 \\ u & 7 & 9\end{aligned}
$$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
\int_{-1}^{0}\frac{2}{2 x + 9}\,\text{d}x=\int_{7}^{9}\frac{1}{u}\cdot 1\,\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve it and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_{7}^{9}\frac{1}{u}\cdot 1\,\text{d}u & =1\int_{7}^{9}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =1\ln(u)|_{7}^{9} \\  & =1(\ln(9)-\ln(7)) \\  & =- \log{\left(7 \right)} + 2 \log{\left(3 \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

generation.domain: a*x^n+b>0 throughout closed original x interval; no poles
